text:
Legislation to relax U.S. export restrictions on computer encoding technology advanced as the House Judiciary Committee approved the measure.
The bill is called the Security and Freedom through Encryption Act.
The bill will be reviewed by the House International Relations Committee.
Opponents of the bill plan to contest it in the House International Relations Committee.
Encryption is a technology that scrambles information, making it unreadable without a password or software key.
The Clinton administration opposes the bill, arguing it could aid international criminals and terrorists.
Representative Bob Goodlatte is the author of the bill.
Goodlatte expressed hope for a compromise with administration officials.
The bill would criminalize the use of encryption to conceal information related to felonies.
Software industry officials and privacy advocates support the legislation and urge lawmakers to continue its progress.

The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) issued forecasts for 1997 on Monday.
The CSU predicted a slight economic upturn for 1997.
The CSU expected real gross domestic product (GDP) growth for 1997 of 4.0-5.0 percent.
The CSU estimated GDP growth of 4.1 percent for 1996.
The CSU forecasted average annual inflation to ease to 7.5-8.0 percent from 8.8 percent.
The CSU projected the current account deficit to grow to 137-145 billion crowns from an estimated 110.6 billion crowns in 1996.
Analysts warned that the widening current account and trade deficits could undermine the economy.
David Lubin, an economist at HSBC Midland, stated that the forecasts were credible but not very encouraging.
The CSU estimated the current account shortfall to be 8.6-9.1 percent of GDP in 1997.
The CSU forecasted the trade deficit to widen to 202-212 billion crowns from a deficit of 160.3 billion crowns in 1996.

China will tighten inspections of imported animals and plants next year for possible diseases.
Chinese quarantine officials banned poultry imports from several U.S. states and a part of Britain.
The China Daily Business Weekly reported that animal and quarantine authorities will carry out stricter inspections.
Inspections will cover imports and exports of plants, animals, fruit, agricultural goods, containers, packages, and other transport materials.
New regulations approved by the State Council will govern these inspections.
Quarantine and customs officials will inspect both hand-carried items and goods imported or exported by traders.
Pets and plants of diplomats with diplomatic immunity will also be inspected.
Authorities could impose fines of up to 50,000 yuan ($6,000) on violators.
China announced a ban on poultry imports from Missouri and Oklahoma due to five cases of Newcastle disease.
The United States denied the accusation and sought talks with China to lift the ban.

USG Corp is a maker of building products such as wallboard.
USG Corp aims to double its earnings by the early 2000s from its 1995 earnings base.
William Foote is the chief executive of USG Corp.
USG Corp reported earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization of $417 million in 1995.
USG Corp's EBITDA rose to $437 million in 1996.
USG Corp plans to achieve its earnings goal through revenue growth from production expansion and cost-cutting initiatives.
USG Corp seeks to have its debt rating raised to investment grade by the end of 1998.
USG Corp currently spends about $150 million a year on capital improvements and $150 million a year to pay down debt.
USG Corp's United States Gypsum Co unit plans to spend at least $85 million to build a facility for manufacturing gypsum wood fiber panels.
USG Corp announced plans to build a new wallboard manufacturing facility in Bridgeport, Ala. for $110 million.

Chrysler Corp. announced that the base price of the redesigned 1997 Jeep Cherokee will be $555 to $1,344 higher than the 1996 model.
The base SE, two-door, two-wheel-drive 1997 Jeep Cherokee will start at $15,825, an increase of $555 from the 1996 model.
The four-door, four-wheel-drive Cherokee Sport model will sell for $20,985, an increase of $815 from the 1996 model.
The four-door, four-wheel-drive Country model will start at $23,945, an increase of $1,344 over the 1996 model.
The Sport and Country models of the 1997 Jeep Cherokee offer a standard six-cylinder engine.
The SE model of the 1997 Jeep Cherokee offers a standard four-cylinder engine.
All prices for the 1997 Jeep Cherokee include a $525 destination charge.
The 1997 Jeep Cherokee features a new instrument panel with dual air bags, updated sheet metal, and a redesigned grille.
Chrysler has the capacity to build about 150,000 Cherokees annually at its Toledo, Ohio, assembly plant.
Through the first 10 months of 1996, Jeep dealers sold 131,995 Cherokees, a 44 percent increase over the 91,246 sold in the same period of 1995.

Cascade Communications Corp reported growth in its core frame-relay business in 1996.
The growth in frame-relay business was partially concealed in other business segments.
Daniel Smith is the chief executive of Cascade Communications Corp.
Some frame-relay business is included in the sales of Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) products.
Daniel Smith expects Cascade to gain frame-relay market share in 1997, but at a slower pace than in 1996.
Cascade grew market share significantly in 1996.
Cascade's policy is not to make specific growth forecasts.
Cascade experienced relatively flat sequential frame-relay sales in the fourth quarter compared to the September quarter.
The flat sales were attributed to delays in telecom customer orders.
Cascade stock fell sharply after the release of its fourth quarter earnings, despite slightly better-than-expected results.

Kenneth Dam is the chairman of a National Research Council report on computer encoding technology.
Dam stated that the report's findings from a year ago are still valid.
Dam is a law professor at the University of Chicago.
Dam told Reuters that a government access approach favored by the Clinton administration is not ready for widespread use.
Encryption is important for online commerce and global communications on the Internet.
Encryption scrambles information and makes it unreadable without a password or software key.
The Clinton administration bars the export of strong encryption unless it includes a key recovery feature.
Key recovery allows the government to decode messages by accessing software keys.
Critics argue that poorly designed key recovery systems could create vulnerabilities for hackers.
Dam echoed the NRC report's findings that key recovery is not sufficiently reliable yet.

Nicola Horlick announced her resignation from Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG) on Thursday.
Horlick described a feeling of turmoil among fund managers at DMG following her resignation.
A spokesman for Horlick stated she planned to take legal action against DMG for constructive dismissal.
Horlick had been suspended pending an internal investigation into a potential breach of her contract.
The dispute involved allegations that Horlick intended to leave and take staff with her.
Last year, MGAM faced a scandal over misvaluations in three of its funds.
Peter Young was sacked from MGAM following the misvaluation scandal.
Horlick's suspension caused unease among large pension fund clients at DMG.
Horlick received a promotion to managing director shortly before her suspension.
Deutsche Bank agreed to a compensation package of around 200 million pounds to address investor losses.

Chinese police have detained dissident Wang Donghai.
Amnesty International has accused the Chinese government of torturing, imprisoning, and killing those who speak out.
Wang's family was informed by police in Hangzhou that he would be sent to a 'study class'.
The term 'study class' is a euphemism for coercive ideological reform.
Two public security officers took Wang away but did not provide a reason for his detention.
Wang's family was not allowed to meet him or know his location.
Wang's sister suspects his detention is related to fellow dissident Chen Longde.
Chen Longde jumped from a third-floor window on August 17 due to mistreatment by a prison official.
Wang and Chen Longde were ordered to serve one year and three years of 're-education through labour', respectively.
Wang was previously jailed for two years for organizing protests after the Tiananmen Square crackdown in 1989.

Harnischfeger Industries Inc is led by chief executive officer Jeffery Glade.
Jeffery Glade believes acquiring Giddings & Lewis Inc is the best option for Harnischfeger.
Giddings & Lewis Inc is based in Fond Du Lac, Wisconsin.
Harnischfeger has made a $747 million unsolicited tender offer for Giddings.
Harnischfeger is seeking other acquisitions regardless of the outcome of the Giddings offer.
Jeffery Glade stated that this is not Harnischfeger's last acquisition in the industrial product service group.
The machine tool and material handling industry is estimated to be worth more than $80 billion.
Jeffery Glade described the industry as poorly served and fragmented.
Giddings is a supplier of industrial automation products and machine tools.
Giddings' board of directors issued a rejection to Harnischfeger's offer, requesting a two-year 'stand still' agreement.

Automakers plan to introduce new sport/utility vehicle models at the North American International Auto Show.
The auto show takes place in Detroit and showcases advancements in size, style, luxury, and refinement of vehicles.
Analysts are particularly interested in Ford Motor Co.'s Lincoln Navigator and Chrysler Corp.'s Dodge Durango.
The Dodge Durango features styling elements from the Dodge Dakota pickup truck.
Subaru is introducing the Forester, a car-based hybrid sport/utility vehicle.
U.S. compact sport/utility vehicle sales grew by 17.9 percent in 1996, totaling 1,575,627 units.
Compact sport/utility vehicles accounted for 11.3 percent of the market in 1996.
Full-size sport/utility vehicles experienced a growth of 51.5 percent in 1996, totaling 379,260 vehicles.
In 1996, trucks, including sport/utility vehicles and minivans, made up 66 percent of Chrysler's total vehicle sales.
Ford's Navigator is based on the F-150 pickup truck and is expected to be priced in the mid-$40,000 range.

Novell Inc outlined a five-year game plan to reduce dependence on its network operating system business.
The plan aims to diversify Novell's revenue base into faster-growing software businesses.
Joseph Marengi is the president and chief operating officer of Novell Inc.
Novell is considering using its $1 billion in cash for selective technology acquisitions.
Marengi stated that Novell's strategy is focused on building its business as a standalone company.
Novell has a market capitalization of $4 billion, $1 billion in cash, and $1.5 billion in revenues.
Marengi indicated that Novell's core NetWare operating systems business is expected to decline to 40 percent of total revenues.
By 2002, Novell expects to generate 25 percent of its revenues from platform-independent products and 25 percent from network applications software.
Novell's strategy includes moving beyond its dominance in the client/server-based local area network market.
Marengi believes Novell will displace Microsoft Corp's Exchange product as the number two electronic messaging product in the world.

The number of banks charging non-customers for using their automated teller machines doubled over the past six months.
About 45 percent of ATMs added a surcharge for non-customers, up from 23 percent in October.
The average fee for using an ATM increased by 20 percent to $1.15 from 96 cents.
Edmund Mierzwinski is the programme director for the U.S. Public Interest Research Group.
Connecticut and Iowa have banned the practice of charging non-customers for ATM use.
Twelve other states and the federal government are considering legislation against ATM surcharges.
The two largest ATM networks, Visa's Plus and Mastercard's Cirrus, lifted a prohibition on surcharges one year ago.
Banks defended the surcharge practice by stating it helps pay for ATMs in new locations.
The American Bankers Association stated that the marketplace should decide ATM prices.
Among the 300 largest banks, 53 percent of ATMs charged a fee, compared to 40 percent of smaller bank ATMs and 6 percent of credit union ATMs.

Morgan Grenfell and former fund manager Nicola Horlick are in a dispute.
Pension fund clients are reassessing their relationships with Morgan Grenfell.
Nicola Horlick resigned from her position after being suspended for an alleged breach of contract.
Horlick is in meetings with legal representatives in London.
Horlick's lawyers stated she seeks an amicable settlement with Morgan Grenfell.
Horlick is prepared to sue if a settlement cannot be reached.
John Farr, a partner at Herbert Smith, mentioned Horlick is hopeful for an amicable resolution.
Details regarding the reasons for Horlick's departure from MGAM are not fully disclosed.
MGAM has initiated a damage-limitation campaign by contacting clients and holding meetings.
The London Borough of Lewisham and Norfolk County Council expressed concerns about recent developments at MGAM.

Papua New Guinea's Australian-listed stocks fell five to ten percent on Monday.
International investors reacted to the army's attempt to force the PNG government aside.
Orogen Minerals Ltd, which is 51 percent owned by the PNG government, fell seven percent to A$3.20.
Other stocks dropped as much as ten percent during afternoon trade.
The head of the army and the police commissioner told Prime Minister Julius Chan to resign or be forced aside in two days.
The army and police are unhappy with the government's employment of mercenaries to subdue secessionists on Bougainville Island.
Brokers and analysts expressed concerns about a potential army mutiny and civil unrest in Port Moresby spreading to remote areas.
Michael Heffernan, a research director at Shaw Stockbroking, warned that local tribes might disrupt mining operations.
Major mining projects in Papua New Guinea often face disputes with local tribal groups.
The Bougainville Copper mine was shut down in 1989 due to landowner sabotage and a revolt.

Case Corp plans to spend $950 million in the next four years to revamp its product line.
Jean-Pierre Rosso is the chief executive of Case Corp, which is based in Racine, Wisconsin.
Case Corp aims to replace all major agricultural products by the end of the century.
Many construction products will also be revamped as part of the overhaul.
A new tractor series, the MX Series, will enter production in the spring.
The MX Series tractors range from 85 to 115 horsepower and represent about 30 percent of tractor sales worldwide for Case.
Orders for the MX Series tractors in the United States and Europe have exceeded company plans.
The MX Series tractors will be produced in Racine and the United Kingdom.
The switch from the German production site is expected to lower costs due to labor and logistics.
The new tractor design utilizes more common components to reduce costs.

General Motors Corp. stock rose on Friday due to optimism about a potential dividend increase and stock buyback programme.
Analysts expect GM's board of directors to announce a stock buyback programme of up to $5 billion.
GM shares increased by $1.125 to $63 after reaching a 52-week high of $63.75 on the New York Stock Exchange.
GM recently sold its Hughes Aircraft defence operations to Raytheon Corp. for $9.5 billion.
Analysts believe GM is trying to catch up with Chrysler Corp. and Ford Motor Co. in returning cash to shareholders.
CS First Boston analyst Nicholas Colas stated that it is time for GM to reward shareholders for their patience.
GM spokeswoman Toni Simonetti confirmed that the board would consider the dividend but did not comment on potential increases or buybacks.
Analysts estimated that GM's board will increase the quarterly dividend by 10 to 20 cents per share.
GM currently pays a quarterly dividend of 40 cents per share.
Analysts noted that GM ended 1996 with $15 billion in cash, which is $3 billion above its target.

NCR Corp. unveiled a prototype for a do-it-yourself retail checkout system on Friday.
The system is designed to speed supermarket checkout times and reduce shopper frustration.
The automated checkout system allows shoppers to scan, bag, and pay for groceries without cashier assistance.
NCR plans to introduce the self-checkout system in 1998 after in-store consumer testing this year.
NCR estimates there are more than 175,000 food store checkout lanes in the United States.
About 30 percent of those lanes are operated as cashier-assisted express lanes.
Joanne Walter, NCR's vice president of future retailing systems, stated the system targets frequent shoppers with a few items.
The initial system is aimed at food store express lanes, with future versions targeting other retail environments.
Walter mentioned that 65 percent of all retail purchases involve 20 items or less.
The automated checkout system is known as SCOT, which stands for Self Checkout Terminal.

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin will explain the Clinton administration's bank reform plan on Capitol Hill.
Lawmakers are expected to focus on what the Clinton plan omitted.
The Clinton proposal aims to eliminate the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act's separation of banking from other financial services.
The Clinton administration did not address the issue of allowing banks to combine with commercial firms.
Rubin announced two alternatives in the Clinton plan and left the decision to Congress.
Congress has been debating changes to U.S. banking laws for over a decade without success.
Opponents of mixing banking and commerce, led by Jim Leach, will question Rubin about the risks of unlimited mergers.
Proponents of mixing banking and commerce, including Marge Roukema and Richard Baker, will support the idea.
One alternative proposed by Rubin allows limited mixing of banking and commerce, excluding the largest nonfinancial firms.
The second alternative maintains the prohibition on mixing but keeps the exception for commercial firms owning savings and loan institutions.

Dresdner Bank and ABN AMRO Holding NV are interested in expanding their presence in the British fund management business.
Analysts have indicated that the acquisition options for these banks will be limited.
The price range for quoted asset management companies varies from around 125 million pounds to several billion pounds.
Top performers like Mercury Asset Management are considered prohibitively expensive.
Major players in the market have not indicated they are available for acquisition.
Weaker fund firms are not likely to attract interest from European banks seeking immediate market impact.
Some banks believe that the prices for asset management businesses are too high.
Insurance companies are also interested in acquiring more asset management business.
New entrants to the asset management field, including retailers and supermarkets, are expected to emerge.
Dresdner Bank announced a restructuring of its global fund management business to include non-German funds.

Australia's largest banks and insurance groups have paused their expansion plans for the past year while awaiting the Wallis report.
The Financial System Inquiry was established in June last year by the Liberal/National government and chaired by Stan Wallis.
The Wallis report is scheduled to be released at noon on Wednesday.
Analysts expect Wallis to recommend easing restrictions on mergers between Australia's six largest financial groups.
National Australia Bank (NAB) is expected to pursue acquisitions of smaller banks like Westpac Banking Corp and ANZ Banking Group Ltd.
One bank announced a takeover of a smaller regional bank before the Wallis report was released.
Treasurer Peter Costello will not approve Westpac's plan to take over Bank of Melbourne until he reviews Wallis' recommendations.
Wallis is expected to ease rules on foreign takeovers of Australia's largest banks and reform prudential supervision systems.
Craig Drummond, head of research at J.B. Were, stated that the expectation is for Wallis to lead to an easing of merger rules.
The 'Six Pillars' policy, instituted by Labor Treasurer Paul Keating in 1990, prevents mergers among Australia's big four banks and two largest insurance groups.

Several days before a report on the Busang gold controversy, Freeport McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc. confirmed it had not found significant gold at the site in Indonesia.
Freeport reported finding 'insignificant amounts' of gold from preliminary tests of Busang last month.
Freeport has continued testing its original seven drill cores taken from the Busang site.
Freeport spokesman Kristin Lemkau stated that the findings from the drill cores are unchanged and that no additional drilling has been done.
Freeport mentioned the continued testing of the drill cores in its first-quarter results but provided no further details.
A Canadian mining analyst suggested that Freeport is ensuring thorough testing to determine the presence of gold.
Freeport's announcement on March 26 caused panic selling of shares in Bre-X Minerals Ltd.
Bre-X Minerals Ltd. lost almost C$3 billion in stock market value last month and its shares have been volatile amid rumors.
Bre-X stock traded at C$3.60 on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Thursday, down C2 cents.
Rumors about Freeport Chief Executive Jim Moffett's resignation and preliminary results from an audit were rejected by Bre-X and Freeport officials.

Kellogg Co. will acquire the Lender's Bagels business from Kraft Foods Inc. for $455 million.
Lender's Bagels is based in White Plains, N.Y.
Lender's Bagels is the largest maker of fresh and frozen bagels sold in grocery stores in the United States.
Lender's Bagels has annual sales of about $275 million.
Kraft Foods Inc. is owned by Philip Morris Cos. Inc.
Kellogg Chairman Arnold Langbo stated that Lender's Bagels is a good fit for Kellogg's convenience foods business.
Analysts believe the acquisition will extend Kellogg's reach into the bagel market, which has annual sales estimated at about $2.8 billion.
Kellogg is the world's largest maker of ready-to-eat breakfast cereal.
Kellogg also produces Pop-Tarts, Eggo waffles, and Nutri-Grain bars.
Standard & Poor's Corp. downgraded Kellogg's corporate debt outlook to negative due to concerns about sales and profits.

3Com Corp. proposed a $6.6 billion acquisition of U.S. Robotics Corp.
The acquisition proposal caused a drop in the stocks of 3Com, U.S. Robotics, and other network companies.
3Com's stock fell $4 to $35 and was the most heavily traded issue on Nasdaq.
More than 40 million shares of 3Com changed hands on Nasdaq.
U.S. Robotics' stock dropped $1.875 to $59.125 and was the second-most active share on Nasdaq.
Analysts claimed the proposed stock swap undervalued U.S. Robotics.
Eric Buck, an analyst at Donaldson Lufkin, criticized the terms of the deal.
The offer involved stock and options valued at $7.3 billion.
Peter Swartz, a Salomon analyst, described the deal as a 'take-under' rather than a takeover.
The merger, if approved, would create a company with $5 billion in annual revenues and 12,000 employees.

The U.S. government is updating thousands of computer systems and software programs to address the year 2000 problem.
Sally Katzen is coordinating the repair effort as the administrator of the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs in the Office of Management and Budget.
Sally Katzen expressed confidence that all major systems will be fixed.
Legislators in Congress are interested in the year 2000 problem and are encouraging agencies to take action.
Some government agencies are aware of the year 2000 problem, while others, such as the air traffic control system, are raising concerns.
Representative Steve Horn stated that Congress will continue to address the year 2000 problem until it is resolved.
Steve Horn is the chairman of the Government Reform Committee's Management, Information and Technology sub-committee.
The sub-committee has received testimony from government and private-sector experts regarding the year 2000 problem.
A recent survey indicated that all government agencies are aware of the year 2000 problem and most are prepared to implement fixes.
The Defence Department and the Social Security Administration have extensive plans to address the year 2000 problem before December 31, 1999.

TrizecHahn Corp is based in Canada.
Dieter Bock is a German businessman.
TrizecHahn Corp and Dieter Bock announced a European property alliance.
Analysts believe the alliance indicates increasing confidence in the UK and European property market.
TrizecHahn has $6.0 billion in assets and $1.2 billion in uncommitted capital.
TrizecHahn plans to buy property projects from Bock's Advanta Management AG for approximately $147 million.
The acquisitions will be financed by issuing subordinate voting shares to Bock, assuming development liabilities, and through construction financing.
Dieter Bock will become president of TrizecHahn Europe and a director of the company with an equity stake of around four percent.
Bock will resign as non-executive deputy chairman of Lonrho Plc and as a director of the British-based trading and hotels conglomerate.
The partnership aims to expand TrizecHahn's operations outside North America.

James Hardie Industries Ltd posted weaker annual profits on Wednesday.
James Hardie forecast that its expanding U.S. fibre cement and gypsum units would drive a profit surge in 1997/98.
Keith Barton is the managing director of James Hardie.
Barton stated that James Hardie has the production capacity to meet U.S. market demand for the first time in several years.
Barton expects strong growth in U.S. sales and earnings to continue in the year ahead if current trading conditions prevail.
James Hardie's net profit increased to A$83 million in the year to March 31 from A$32.2 million in 1995/96.
The increase in net profit was largely due to a A$31.7 million abnormal profit from asset sales.
Profit before abnormals fell 12.3 percent to A$51.3 million due to lower Australasian building materials profits.
James Hardie's Australian operations reported a pre-tax loss of A$800,000 in 1996/97, down from a profit of A$33.8 million in 1995/96.
New Zealand profits fell eight percent to A$31.9 million.

Toronto is Canada's largest city.
A citizens revolt has emerged against Ontario's ruling Conservatives.
Ontario's Conservative Premier is Mike Harris.
Harris proposes merging Toronto and six neighboring municipalities into a single 'megacity'.
The proposed 'megacity' would have a population of 2.4 million people.
The new city would represent about 8 percent of Canada's total population of 30 million.
Harris plans to change how public services are delivered and funded.
Opponents of the plan fear it will increase taxes and lead to urban decay.
Toronto mayor Barbara Hall stated that government is elected by the people for the people.
The recent referendum showed that residents voted three to one against the merger.

Britain's double-decker bus is involved in environmental experiments.
A London bus operator has collaborated with inventor Hassan Assali for two years.
Hassan Assali claims to have a solution for diesel-based pollution fumes.
Assali's invention is an oil recycler that reportedly cuts pollution levels by 50 percent.
The oil recycler saves lubricating oil by recycling it six to ten times.
Assali is the managing director of Pinmore, the company behind the recycler.
The Pinmore recycler prototype was developed over six years with significant investment.
The recycler is manufactured in Huzhan province, China, and has sold 6,000 units.
Customers include an Algerian bus company and Saudi Arabia's frontier guards.
MTL publicly endorsed the recycler after successful tests on its buses.

Computer Associates International Inc shares fell six percent on Wednesday.
Analysts attributed the decline to concerns over a secular decline in mainframe revenues.
The company had previously warned that revenues were unlikely to meet expectations due to sales issues in Europe.
By midday Wednesday, the stock price had decreased by three points to 43.
The stock was the second most active issue on the NYSE.
Analysts noted that CA's decline may be related to broader weakness in the mainframe market.
International Business Machines Corp reported disappointing growth in its hardware business during the December quarter.
IBM is the world's dominant supplier of mainframe software.
Computer Associates is a leading independent supplier of software for mainframe machines.
Analyst Chris Mortenson reported that mainframe revenues had fallen eight percent in the December quarter.

The Prague Stock Exchange's 1997 bull run halted on Thursday as investors took profits.
Analysts predicted that prices would continue falling in the short-term.
The PX50 index closed at 613.6 on Thursday, down 14.0 points or 2.23 percent.
The PX50 index had reached a two-year high of 629.0 on Tuesday.
SPT Telecom a.s., CEZ a.s., and Komercni Banka a.s. were the three biggest issues leading the market lower.
Each of the three biggest issues fell more than 2.2 percent at the fix.
Jan Sykora of brokers Wood and Company stated that the market is thin and profit-taking causes it to collapse.
Analysts expect Komercni Banka a.s. to be hardest hit among blue chips after rising over 25 percent since the start of the year.
Komercni Banka a.s. closed down 4.9 percent on Thursday.
Czech authorities are taking steps to increase transparency and boost investor confidence in the capital markets.

Britain's opposition Labour party stated that problems at Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM) could have been uncovered earlier.
Alistair Darling, shadow chief secretary to the Treasury, expressed that the problem was not determined as soon as it should have been.
Darling warned that alarm bells ought to be ringing in all major financial institutions.
Trading in three funds worth an estimated 1.4 billion pounds was suspended when MGAM disclosed suspected irregularities.
The problems at MGAM are related to the valuation of speculative unlisted high-technology stocks held in the funds.
Trading in the three funds resumed after a 180 million pound cash injection by Deutsche Bank.
Peter Young, the fund manager of two of the funds, was suspended and an injunction was obtained to freeze his assets.
An in-depth probe by the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO) is underway to determine compensation for 90,000 investors.
Darling indicated that the problems at MGAM highlighted imperfections in the regulatory system.
The Labour party will not make recommendations on the latest episode until IMRO completes its investigation.

Australian Treasurer Peter Costello announced that he would not allow a big bank merger until parts of the banking sector became more competitive.
Costello's announcement affected the takeover premium built into Westpac Banking Corp's share price.
National Australia Bank's share price increased by 2.5 percent following Costello's announcement.
Investors were pleased that National Australia Bank would not have to issue shares to finance a takeover.
A senior Sydney bank analyst stated that the market viewed National Australia Bank's situation positively due to the avoidance of share dilution.
Macquarie Equities analyst Graham Maloney noted that National Australia Bank was previously underpriced.
National Australia Bank closed at A$16.11 after Costello's announcement.
Westpac Banking Corp closed down at A$6.67, while ANZ Banking Group Ltd closed down at A$7.89.
Analysts indicated that Costello's comments about ending the ban on foreign takeovers could mitigate some disappointment in the sector.
J.B. Were, head of research at Craig Drummond, mentioned that Westpac and ANZ were not expensive by global standards.

Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc. withdrew from the Busang gold project.
The withdrawal occurred after an independent report on Busang was released by Bre-X Minerals Ltd.
Freeport's own test results from the Busang site were poor.
The report by Strathcona Mineral Services Ltd. confirmed Freeport's findings.
The Busang discovery was claimed by Bre-X to be the richest find of the century.
The Strathcona report stated that the falsification of data was unprecedented in mining history.
Strathcona found evidence of tampering with Bre-X's core samples.
Strathcona's tests revealed only trace amounts of gold at the Busang site.
Freeport's Chief Executive Jim Bob Moffett expressed disappointment over the findings.
Nusamba Group, linked to Indonesian President Suharto, also withdrew from the Busang project.

British defence to electronics giant General Electric Company signalled a shift away from the management legacy of ex-chief Lord Weinstock.
Zafar Khan, an analyst at SocGen, stated that GEC has created a flatter structure with divisional heads reporting directly to George Simpson.
George Simpson succeeded Lord Weinstock as managing director of GEC in September.
GEC announced it would halve the number of its corporate divisions to five key business units: GEC Alsthom, GEC Marconi, GPT, GEC USA, and the industrial group of businesses.
The newly separated industrial group includes the industrial apparatus unit.
GEC created a central committee with representatives from finance, legal affairs, strategic planning, personnel affairs, marketing, and technical issues.
Analysts believe the move updated GEC's corporate structure and created a clearer chain of command.
GEC grouped together its main U.S. businesses, including Picker International, Gilbarco, and Videojet.
An analyst reported that the regrouping did not necessarily indicate that industrials were being separated for sale.
GEC finance director David Newlands stated that the group had received multiple offers mostly above book value.

The Czech December trade deficit is expected to rise to 16 billion crowns ($575 million) from 14.3 billion in November 1995.
The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) will release the 1996 trade figures at 9 a.m. (0800 GMT) on Monday.
Most economists surveyed expect steady growth in the trade deficit with few surprises.
Martin Kupka, an economist at Patria Finance, stated that he expects the figures to align with the development throughout 1996.
The full-year trade gap for 1996 is guaranteed to be a record, as the January-November figure reached 140.1 billion crowns.
The 1995 record total shortfall was 95.7 billion crowns.
Most analysts predict a December trade gap of 15-17 billion crowns, following a 16.6 billion crown shortfall in November.
The consensus forecast for the 1996 trade deficit is between 155-165 billion crowns.
The foreign exchange and money markets are expected to show little reaction to the trade figures unless they significantly differ from estimates.
Czech exporters indicated a desire for a 20 to 25 percent devaluation of the crown to boost exports in 1997.

China is involved in a dispute between North Korea and South Korea.
A North Korean official, Hwang Jang-yop, is seeking asylum at the South Korean embassy in Beijing.
South Korea claims that Hwang Jang-yop and an assistant are seeking asylum.
North Korea accused South Korea of kidnapping Hwang Jang-yop.
North Korea urged China to resolve the situation in its favor.
Diplomats believe it is unlikely for China to resolve the dispute without disappointing North Korea.
Hwang Jang-yop is one of 11 secretaries on the secretariat of North Korea's ruling Workers' Party.
South Korea sent Kim Ha-jung to Beijing for discussions regarding Hwang's asylum.
Chinese police blocked access to South Korea's consular office in Beijing for security reasons.
Hwang Jang-yop is the highest-ranking North Korean official to seek asylum in South Korea.

Brierley Investments Ltd is an investment group based in New Zealand.
Brierley Investments Ltd called on the Australian government to relax its investment rules.
Brierley Investments Ltd wants New Zealand companies to be treated the same as Australian companies in terms of investment.
Brierley chairman Bob Matthew stated that Australia should change its rules to allow New Zealand investment into Australia.
Matthew expressed that there is no merit in having one market for trade and two distinct markets for investment in Australasia.
Brierley Investments has made major investments in Australian companies over the last two to three years.
Brierley Investments owns 28 percent of James Hardie Industries Ltd, 7.4 percent of Coles Myer Ltd, and 19.9 percent of John Fairfax Holdings Ltd.
Brierley Investments has A$1.8 billion invested in Australia and A$1.6 billion in New Zealand.
Brierley Investments faced restrictions that stalled its investment push in Australia this year.
Matthew indicated that he is not optimistic about the Australian government changing its investment regulations.

Strippers can dance naked in Canada as long as they maintain distance from customers.
The Supreme Court of Canada ruled that lap dancing is indecent and a criminal act.
Exotic dancers cheered the Supreme Court ruling that bans lap dancing.
Club owners warned that the ban on lap dancing could deter customers and harm businesses.
A dancer at Filmores stated that dancing is for seeing, not touching.
Andy, a patron at the Zanzibar strip club, claimed the court ban on lap dancing was unnecessary.
Lap dancing became widespread in Canada after a 1994 Ontario judge's ruling that it did not offend community standards.
Katharine Goldberg, a former stripper, led a campaign against lap dancing, claiming it forced dancers into degrading acts.
Some strippers expressed resentment towards Goldberg's portrayal of them as sex slaves.
The Supreme Court upheld an appeal court decision that stated lap dancing degraded dancers and encouraged objectification.

Britain could raise between 600 million and 1.5 billion pounds from the sale of the London Underground rail network, according to Steven Norris.
Steven Norris is a former transport minister and is currently working on the Conservative Party election manifesto.
Norris is leading the Conservative Party's election campaign for London and the south-east of England.
Norris stated that the government is examining fare and service standard controls for the tube network.
Norris has been involved informally with government studies regarding a possible sale of the tube network.
The sale proceeds figure mentioned by Norris excludes the cost of necessary investments.
The gross proceeds figure for the sale of the tube network is estimated to be between 1.4 billion and 2.5 billion pounds.
London Underground has become a significant political issue in the lead-up to Britain's general election.
There is pressure on the government to present a compelling case to the public regarding the sale of the tube.
Labour leader Tony Blair has stated his commitment to keeping the tube in public hands and revitalizing it through private sector investment.

The Czech Republic reached the final of Euro '96.
Czech supporters are unhappy with recent changes in football broadcasting.
Supporters have expressed nostalgia for the time under Communism.
The Czech-Moravian Football Association (CMFS) announced plans to cancel live broadcasts of matches on public television starting in 1998.
CMFS will broadcast only pay-per-view first division matches in the 1998-99 season.
The pay-per-view broadcasting agreement was signed with the Dutch firm Nethold.
Jaroslav Vacek, of STES, stated that soccer is now treated as a business rather than public entertainment.
The broadcasting deal is believed to be worth about 100 million crowns ($3.7 million) annually.
The deal is expected to increase television revenues by about 80 percent for each of the first division's 16 clubs.
Since the fall of communism in 1989, Czech soccer has experienced a mass exodus of athletes seeking better opportunities in the West.

China's leadership has dissolved the personal office of Deng Xiaoping.
Deng Xiaoping is 92 years old.
The dissolution of Deng's office may indicate his health is fragile.
Deng's health has caused speculation affecting stock markets in China, Hong Kong, and Taiwan.
Japanese media reported that Deng was admitted to the hospital in critical condition.
A Hong Kong newspaper stated that Deng was recuperating at home from a brain hemorrhage.
China's official media did not report on Deng's health.
The Deng office was dissolved shortly before the Lunar New Year on February 7.
Jiang Zemin and Premier Li Peng returned to Beijing to visit Deng.
Deng has not been seen in public since the 1994 Chinese Lunar New Year festival.

Talks between Caterpillar Inc. and the United Auto Workers will resume with the help of a federal mediator.
The talks will be the first formal negotiations since November 1995.
A tentative agreement was submitted to UAW members in November 1995 but was subsequently rejected.
The 17-month strike ended in December 1995 without a new contract.
Caterpillar's workers have been without a contract since 1991.
John Calhoun Wells is the FMCS director.
Jobs and job security have been main issues throughout negotiations.
Almost 400 unfair labour practice complaints by the UAW have been filed.
Caterpillar reported a profit of $1.4 billion on revenues of $16.52 billion in 1996.
Caterpillar shares rose $2.625 to $93.

Bre-X Minerals Ltd announced that a key report on the Busang gold mystery will be released before North American financial markets open on Monday.
Strathcona Mineral Services Ltd. is the consulting firm hired by Bre-X to audit the Busang project.
Strathcona is expected to issue an interim report on its findings to Bre-X by Friday.
Bre-X expects to release the interim report next Monday morning prior to the opening of financial markets in North America.
Bre-X spokesman Richard Wool stated that reports about an elaborate press conference in Toronto for the announcement are incorrect.
Rumors about Busang intensified after Freeport-McMoRan Copper and Gold Inc. reported on March 26 that its preliminary tests found insignificant amounts of gold.
Panic selling of Bre-X shares resulted in a loss of almost C$3 billion or 80 percent of the company's stock market value.
Bre-X was previously estimated to contain 71 million ounces of gold at the Busang site.
Bre-X shares closed up C15 cents at C$3.80 on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Tuesday.
Freeport chief executive Jim Bob Moffett stated that the company hopes the Strathcona report will provide more clarity on the Busang situation.

Eurotunnel Plc assured investors that the financial fallout from last November's fire would not impact its debt rescue plan or long-term growth.
Eurotunnel stated that the November fire should not significantly affect the company's long-term financial performance.
Eurotunnel indicated that there would be no need to review the financial restructuring plan due to the fire.
The fire caused a partial shutdown and reduced services in one of the cross-channel tunnels.
Eurotunnel reported that sales had survived the fire, with passenger numbers sharply increasing.
Richard Hannah, an analyst at UBS, stated that the key message for investors is that the refinancing will not need to be restructured.
A special shareholder meeting to consider the debt refinancing was initially scheduled for April but has been delayed to June.
Eurotunnel's banking syndicate requested an extension of the debt standstill arrangement to December.
Eurotunnel reported an estimated turnover of 450 million pounds for 1996, up from 300 million in 1995.
Thirteen million passengers traveled through the tunnel in 1996, an increase from eight million the previous year.

East European markets increased this week due to key foreign investors pushing prices higher.
The Warsaw and Budapest bourses reached year-highs.
Exchanges in Romania and Ljubljana also experienced significant gains.
Shares in Bratislava and Prague saw slight increases but lacked upward momentum.
The Warsaw Stock Exchange achieved three consecutive 33-month highs this week.
Heavy turnover was noted on the Warsaw Stock Exchange.
Analysts predict a profit-taking correction may occur next week.
The Warsaw bourse has risen 23 percent since December 10.
Analysts expect 16,000 points to provide strong support for the WIG index next week.
The Budapest bourse set record highs in the first three sessions of the week.

China vowed to intensify a crackdown on economic disorder in 1997.
The crackdown is in response to tax evasion, financial irregularities, smuggling, and counterfeiting.
These economic issues cost the state billions of dollars a year.
The official People's Daily stated that the situation of economic disorder has not changed.
Chinese authorities uncovered tax, auditing, and pricing violations valued at 161 billion yuan over the past 11 years.
This amounts to an average of 14.6 billion yuan a year.
The commentary emphasized the importance of regulating and revamping economic order.
Tax evasion and smuggling increased alongside market-oriented economic reforms introduced by Deng Xiaoping in the late 1970s.
State media reported that taxpayers evaded personal income tax worth an estimated 12 billion yuan since 1980.
Up to 60 percent of state-run or collective firms in China evaded taxes.

Vin Gupta is the founder and chief executive officer of American Business Information Inc.
Vin Gupta supported the First Call consensus forecast of $0.23 a share in third quarter earnings from continuing operations.
Vin Gupta also supported the forecast of $0.91 a share for the full year.
The estimates for the third quarter of 1995 were $0.20 a share and $0.80 a share for all of 1995.
American Business Information Inc. sells data to customers for sales leads.
Vin Gupta stated that while the information is publicly available, it is not easy for individual businesses to find.
Vin Gupta purchased about 200,000 shares of the company on July 16.
American Business Information Inc. bought back about 200,000 shares under a stock repurchase plan approved in June.
Vin Gupta and his family own 56 percent of the company's stock.
Vin Gupta expects sales of about $100 million in 1996, compared to $86.8 million in 1995.

General Motors Corp. experienced a loss of 1.3 percentage points in U.S. market share in 1996.
Chairman Jack Smith announced plans to aggressively increase U.S. market share in 1997.
GM is the world's largest automaker.
In the 1960s, GM commanded half of the U.S. market.
As of the mid-1980s, GM held as much as 45 percent of the U.S. passenger car market.
In 1996, GM's U.S. light vehicle sales fell 2.7 percent to 4.74 million units.
GM's market share dropped to 31.3 percent in 1996 from 32.6 percent in 1995 and 33.1 percent in 1994.
Costly labor strikes in March and October 1996 hurt GM's market share.
The strikes cost GM an estimated $1.2 billion to $1.3 billion in profits and resulted in the loss of about 300,000 vehicles.
GM expects to utilize more than 90 percent of its North American factory capacity in 1997 if labor relations are peaceful.

Britain's opposition Labour Party outlined its transport blueprint on Tuesday.
Labour pledged no sell-off of the London Underground system.
Labour proposed a partnership with the private sector on investment.
Labour announced a review of rail and bus regulation.
Labour leader Tony Blair supported a public-private partnership for the metro system.
Blair stated that the partnership would provide an alternative to wholesale privatisation.
Shadow transport secretary Andrew Smith shifted away from the interventionist policies of his predecessor Clare Short.
Labour's revised transport vision promised tougher regulation without reversing the rail sell-off.
Smith proposed using the private sector for investment in track maintenance and new trains.
Labour plans to push policies for less road building and more traffic management.
